hints: Think about the word closed first. Where is the blood at all times - does it ever leave tubes to bathe tissues directly?
Now think about the word double. How many times does blood go through the heart in one full trip around the body, and what are the two separate loops called?
walkthrough:
What Closed Really Means**
Blood never leaves the plumbing. In mammals it stays inside the heart and blood vessels - arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins. Tissue fluid leaks out at capillaries, but red blood cells and most plasma stay inside. This is different from an open system in insects where blood bathes organs directly.

What Double Really Means**
Follow one red blood cell. From the heart it goes to the lungs, back to the heart, then out to the body, then back to the heart again. That is two loops: pulmonary circulation (heart to lungs and back for oxygenation) and systemic circulation (heart to body and back to deliver oxygen). So blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit.

Final answer: Closed means blood is always contained within blood vessels (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries) and does not bathe tissues directly. Double means there are two circulations - pulmonary (heart to lungs and back) and systemic (heart to rest of body and back) - so blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit.

hints: Start at 1 - pulmonary vein. Remember veins carry blood toward the heart, and the pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left side of the heart. Which left chamber pumps it out next?

Trace the systemic loop forward. After the left ventricle pumps into the largest artery, blood goes to the body, then returns in the largest vein to the right side. Put aorta, vena cava and right atrium in that flow order.
walkthrough:
From Lungs Into the Pump**
Pulmonary vein (1) brings oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium, which passes it to the left ventricle. So left ventricle is 2. The left ventricle is thick-walled because it must generate high pressure to push blood around the whole body.

Out to Body and Back to Right Side**
Left ventricle pumps into the aorta (3), the main artery to the body. After delivering oxygen, deoxygenated blood returns via the vena cava (4) into the right atrium (5). That completes the systemic part of the sequence: 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 to 5.
Final answer: pulmonary vein 1; left ventricle 2; aorta 3; vena cava 4; right atrium 5.

hints: Compare the blood pressure just after leaving the ventricles with the low pressure returning in veins. Which vessel must stretch and not burst?
Link wall structure to function. Which layer is thicker in arteries and what two tissues in it allow stretching, recoil and maintaining pressure?
walkthrough:
Pressure Is the Problem**
Blood leaves the ventricles in surges at high pressure. Arteries are closest to this push, so their walls must withstand the pressure without bursting or tearing. Veins carry blood back at much lower pressure, so they can have thin walls.

How Thickness Solves It**
The extra thickness is mainly tunica media with more elastic fibres and smooth muscle. Elastic fibres stretch when pressure rises and recoil to push blood onward and smooth out flow. Smooth muscle can contract to help maintain pressure. Together they protect the vessel and keep blood moving.

Final answer: Arteries carry blood at much higher pressure than veins. Thicker walls, especially thicker tunica media with more elastic fibres and smooth muscle, withstand high pressure and prevent rupturing and help maintain blood pressure and flow.

hints: Start with carbon monoxide in the lungs. It competes with oxygen for the same binding site on haemoglobin - what stable compound does it form?
Think about the consequence for oxygen transport if some haemoglobin is blocked. What happens to oxygen carrying capacity and delivery to tissues?
Now switch to nicotine as a stimulant. If the heart beats faster and small arteries narrow, what must happen to blood pressure?
Remember clotting risk. How does nicotine change platelet behaviour and vessel lining to favour thrombosis and higher blood pressure?
walkthrough:
Carbon Monoxide Blocks Oxygen Transport**
Carbon monoxide diffuses into red blood cells and binds to haemoglobin where oxygen would bind, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. Haemoglobin has a much higher affinity for carbon monoxide than for oxygen, so even small amounts block a lot of haemoglobin.

Less Oxygen Reaches Tissues**
With haemoglobin occupied, less oxygen can be carried. That means reduced percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen and reduced oxygen carrying capacity of the blood. Tissues receive less oxygen, so the heart may have to work harder.

Nicotine Speeds Up and Squeezes**
Nicotine stimulates the nervous system. It increases heart rate and causes vasoconstriction of arteries and arterioles. Narrower vessels plus faster pumping raises blood pressure. Higher pressure puts more strain on vessel walls and the heart.

Nicotine Favours Clots**
Nicotine makes platelets sticky, promoting blood clotting and thrombosis which can block coronary arteries. Both carbon monoxide and nicotine can also damage the endothelium, the smooth lining of vessels, which further increases risk of atheroma and clot formation.

Final answer: Carbon monoxide: binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing haemoglobin available to bind oxygen and reducing oxygen carrying capacity / percentage saturation of blood. Nicotine: increases heart rate and blood pressure, constricts arteries / arterioles (vasoconstriction) and makes platelets sticky promoting clotting / thrombosis. Either substance can damage endothelium / lining of vessels.
